items.prose: A bakery's daily profit, in pounds, when it bakes $x$ trays of bread is $P(x) = -5x^2 + 60x - 100$. Its graph is a parabola.

parts.question: Where does the graph of $P$ cross the vertical axis? Give $P(0)$ in pounds, as a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $x = 0$ into every term of the rule.

byKey.sign: The rule ends in $-100$, so $P(0) = -100$: with no bread baked the bakery loses £100.
byKey.zero: The squared and the $60x$ terms are 0 at $x = 0$, but the $-100$ stays.

explain.text: At $x = 0$ every term with an $x$ is 0, so the y-intercept is $P(0) = -100$. The bakery loses £100 a day, its fixed costs, if it bakes nothing.

parts.question: The rule factorises as $P(x) = -5(x - 2)(x - 10)$. At which numbers of trays does the bakery break even, $P(x) = 0$? Give both, separated by a comma.

feedback.correct: A product is 0 only when a factor is: $x - 2 = 0$ or $x - 10 = 0$, so $x = 2$ or $x = 10$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Set each bracket equal to 0.

byKey.fives: The $-5$ in front is never 0, so it gives no root. The roots come from the brackets: 2 and 10.
byKey.count: The graph crosses the horizontal axis twice, so give two values.

explain.text: The roots are where the curve crosses the horizontal axis. $-5(x - 2)(x - 10)$ is 0 when $x = 2$ or $x = 10$. Check: $P(2) = -20 + 120 - 100 = 0$.

parts.question: Using the roots 2 and 10, at what $x$ is the turning point of the parabola? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: The turning point is halfway between the roots: $(2 + 10) \div 2 = 6$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A parabola is symmetric, so its turning point sits halfway between its roots.

byKey.half-top: You halved 10. Halfway between 2 and 10 is $(2 + 10) \div 2 = 6$.
byKey.half-gap: 4 is half the gap between the roots. Add it to the lower root: $2 + 4 = 6$.

explain.text: A parabola is mirrored about a vertical line through its turning point. The roots 2 and 10 sit the same distance either side of it. So the turning point is at $(2 + 10) \div 2 = 6$.

parts.question: Using $x = 6$, what is the greatest daily profit, in pounds? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $x = 6$ into the rule and work each term in turn.

byKey.from-five: That is $P(5)$. The top is at $x = 6$: $P(6) = 80$.
byKey.from-four: That is $P(4)$. The top is at $x = 6$: $P(6) = 80$.
byKey.sign-square: You added $5 \times 36$. The term is $-5x^2$, so take off 180.

explain.text: The $-5$ in front makes the parabola an upside-down U, so its turning point is a highest point. $P(6) = -180 + 360 - 100 = 80$. The best the bakery can make is £80 a day.

parts.question: Using the turning point at $x = 6$, where is the graph of $P$ increasing?

options.why: That is where it falls. An upside-down U rises up to its top, then falls.
That is where the profit is positive. Increasing means rising as you move right.
Past 10 the profit is negative and still falling.

feedback.correct: The curve is an upside-down U with its top at $x = 6$, so it rises for $x < 6$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Picture the upside-down U and move along it from left to right.

explain.text: An upside-down U goes up as you move right until its top, then comes down. The top is at $x = 6$. So $P$ is increasing for $x < 6$ and decreasing for $x > 6$.

items.prose: A sledge starts from rest at the top of a slope just as a cyclist rolls past at a steady 3 m/s. After $t$ seconds the sledge has gone $s = 0.5t^2$ metres and the cyclist $c = 3t$ metres.

parts.question: How far has the sledge gone after 4 seconds? Give a whole number of metres.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Square the 4 first, then halve it.

byKey.no-square: You worked out $0.5 \times 4$. The rule squares $t$ first: $4^2 = 16$.
byKey.no-half: That is $4^2$. The rule halves it: $0.5 \times 16 = 8$.

explain.text: Follow the rule in order: square, then halve. $4^2 = 16$ and $0.5 \times 16 = 8$ metres.

parts.question: Using 8 m in 4 seconds, what is the sledge's average speed over those 4 seconds, in m/s? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: Average speed is distance over time: $8 \div 4 = 2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the distance by the time it took.

byKey.times: You multiplied, $8 \times 4$. Speed is distance over time: $8 \div 4$.
byKey.distance: 8 m is the distance. Divide by the 4 seconds for the speed.

explain.text: The average speed is the gradient of the straight line from $(0, 0)$ to $(4, 8)$. That is $8 \div 4 = 2$ m/s, slower than the cyclist so far.

parts.question: The sledge catches the cyclist where the graphs of $s = 0.5t^2$ and $c = 3t$ meet. Solve $0.5t^2 = 3t$ for $t > 0$. Give a whole number of seconds.

feedback.correct: Divide both sides by $t$, which is not 0: $0.5t = 3$, so $t = 6$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Both sides have a factor $t$. Divide it out, since $t > 0$.

byKey.lost-t: You solved $0.5t^2 = 3$. The right-hand side is $3t$, so divide both sides by $t$ first.

explain.text: The graphs meet at $t = 0$, the start, and once more. For $t > 0$ divide by $t$: $0.5t = 3$, so $t = 6$. Check: $0.5 \times 36 = 18$ and $3 \times 6 = 18$.

parts.question: Using $t = 6$, how far have both gone when they meet? Give a whole number of metres.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $t = 6$ into either rule.

byKey.no-half: That is $6^2$. The sledge's rule halves it: $0.5 \times 36 = 18$.

explain.text: At the meeting point both graphs have the same height. $3 \times 6 = 18$ and $0.5 \times 36 = 18$, so both have gone 18 metres.

parts.question: Both have gone 18 m in 6 seconds, so both averaged 3 m/s. At $t = 6$, which is moving faster?

options.text: The sledge: its graph keeps getting steeper
Neither: the graphs cross, so the gradients are equal
options.why: Crossing means equal heights, not equal gradients. The curve is steeper than the line there.

options.text: The cyclist: it was ahead for all 6 seconds
options.why: Being ahead is the height of the graph. Speed is its gradient.

options.text: Neither: their average speeds are both 3 m/s
options.why: Equal averages do not mean equal speeds at the end. The sledge started slower, so it ends faster.

feedback.correct: The sledge's curve gets steeper all the way. Its average over 6 seconds is 3 m/s, so at $t = 6$ it is moving faster than 3 m/s.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Speed is the gradient of the graph at that moment, not its height.

explain.text: On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed. The sledge started at 0 m/s and sped up, yet averaged 3 m/s. So at $t = 6$ its speed is above 3 m/s, and its curve crosses the cyclist's line from below.

items.prose: Two lab cultures are counted every hour. Culture N starts at 200 cells and doubles each hour: $N = 200 \times 2^t$. Culture M starts at 1000 cells and gains 300 an hour: $M = 1000 + 300t$.

parts.question: How many cells are in culture N after 3 hours? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each hour doubles the count, so double 200 three times.

byKey.times-three: You worked out $200 \times 2 \times 3$. The power means doubling three times: $2^3 = 8$.
byKey.two-doublings: You doubled twice. After 3 hours there are three doublings: $200 \to 400 \to 800 \to 1600$.

explain.text: The $t$ is in the power, so each hour doubles the count. $200 \to 400 \to 800 \to 1600$, which is $200 \times 2^3$.

parts.question: Using $N = 1600$ at 3 hours, how many more cells does culture M have than culture N then? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out $M$ at $t = 3$, then take off 1600.

byKey.m-value: 1900 is culture M itself. Take N away: $1900 - 1600 = 300$.

explain.text: $M = 1000 + 900 = 1900$ cells at 3 hours. So M is still ahead, by $1900 - 1600 = 300$.

parts.question: At 4 hours $N = 3200$ and $M = 2200$. Using part 2, how many times do the graphs of N and M cross for $t \ge 0$?

options.why: N is behind at 3 hours but ahead by 1000 at 4 hours. The graphs must cross in between.

options.text: Twice: once on the way up and once later
options.why: Once N is ahead, each doubling adds more than 300, so M never catches up again.
At 3 hours M still leads by 300, so the crossing comes later.

feedback.correct: M leads at 3 hours and N leads at 4, so the graphs cross between them. After that N grows faster, so they never cross again.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare who leads at 3 hours and at 4 hours.

explain.text: M leads by 300 at 3 hours, and N leads by 1000 at 4 hours. So the graphs cross in between. A doubling curve grows ever faster than a line climbing 300 an hour, so N then stays ahead.

parts.question: Using the crossing between 3 and 4 hours, try $t = 3.3$ and $t = 3.4$. Estimate when $200 \times 2^t = 1000 + 300t$. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: At $t = 3.3$, $N \approx 1970$ and $M = 1990$, so M still leads. At $t = 3.4$, $N \approx 2111$ and $M = 2020$, so the crossing is $t \approx 3.3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out N and M at 3.3 and at 3.4 and see which leads.

byKey.midway: 3.5 is halfway between the hours. At 3.4 N already leads, so the crossing is earlier.
byKey.whole-hour: At 3 hours M still leads by 300. Try 3.3 and 3.4 to narrow it down.
byKey.too-late: At 3.4, N leads by about 90. At 3.3, M leads by only about 20, so the crossing is nearer 3.3.

explain.text: At 3.3 M leads by about 20 and at 3.4 N leads by about 90. So the graphs cross just after 3.3, at about $t = 3.32$. To 1 decimal place that is $t \approx 3.3$.

parts.question: Using $t = 3.3$, about how many cells does each culture have when the counts match? Give your answer to the nearest hundred.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Put $t = 3.3$ into either rule and round to the nearest hundred.

byKey.at-three: That is M at 3 hours. The counts match at about 3.3 hours: $1000 + 990 = 1990$.
byKey.at-four: That is M at 4 hours. The counts match at about 3.3 hours: $1000 + 990 = 1990$.
byKey.n-at-three: That is N at 3 hours. The counts match later, at about 3.3 hours.

explain.text: The line is easier: $M = 1000 + 300 \times 3.3 = 1990$. The curve gives $N = 200 \times 2^{3.3} \approx 1970$. Both round to 2000 cells.

items.prose: A toy train track rises and dips. At $x$ metres along, its height above the floor is $h(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x$ centimetres, for $0 \le x \le 4$.

parts.question: Start a table of values for this cubic. What is $h(2)$? Give a whole number of centimetres.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out $2^3$, $6 \times 2^2$ and $9 \times 2$, then combine them with their signs.

byKey.all-plus: You added every term. The middle term is $-6x^2$, so take off 24: $8 - 24 + 18 = 2$.

parts.question: The rule factorises as $h(x) = x(x - 3)^2$. Where does the track meet the floor, $h(x) = 0$? Give both $x$-values, separated by a comma.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set each factor equal to 0.

byKey.signs: Check the sign. $x - 3 = 0$ gives $x = 3$, and $-3$ is off the track anyway.
byKey.count: The track meets the floor at two places: one from the factor $x$ and one from $(x - 3)^2$. Give both, separated by a comma.

explain.text: A product is 0 only when a factor is. The factor $x$ gives $x = 0$ and the factor $(x - 3)^2$ gives $x = 3$. So the roots are 0 and 3.

parts.question: The turning points are at $x = 1$ and $x = 3$, and $h(3) = 0$ from part 2. Where is the track going down?

options.why: There it climbs from $h(0) = 0$ to its top at $x = 1$.
After touching the floor at 3 it climbs again, to $h(4) = 4$.
It climbs first, up to the turning point at $x = 1$, and only then falls.

feedback.correct: The track climbs to a top at $x = 1$, falls to the floor at $x = 3$, then climbs again. So it goes down for $1 < x < 3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Between two turning points the track either rises or falls the whole way.

explain.text: A cubic with a positive $x^3$ rises, turns down, then turns up again. Here it rises to $x = 1$, falls to $h(3) = 0$ and rises after. So it is decreasing for $1 < x < 3$.

parts.question: The top at $x = 1$ has height $h(1) = 4$. Using the flat line $y = 4$, which $x$-values with $0 \le x \le 4$ solve $h(x) = 4$? Give both, separated by a comma.

feedback.correct: The line $y = 4$ touches the curve at the top, $x = 1$, and meets it again at the end: $h(4) = 64 - 96 + 36 = 4$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find where the flat line $y = 4$ meets the curve, and check each value in the rule.

byKey.roots: 0 and 3 solve $h(x) = 0$. Here the flat line is $y = 4$, not the floor.
byKey.turns: 1 and 3 are the turning points, but $h(3) = 0$. The line $y = 4$ meets the curve again at $x = 4$.
byKey.count: The line $y = 4$ meets the curve twice on the track: at the top and at the far end.

explain.text: Draw $y = 4$ across the graph. It touches the curve at the top, $x = 1$, and meets it again where the curve climbs back up. $h(4) = 64 - 96 + 36 = 4$, so the solutions are 1 and 4.
